title: Vector Search Is Now A Data Type, But The Money Math Has Not Gone Away
gist: The standalone vector database category has largely dissolved as ANN search became a native data type in Postgres, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, ClickHouse, MongoDB and Redis, but the underlying cost is unchanged: it's dominated by in-memory HNSW graph size (roughly 1.1x(4xdimension+8xM) bytes per vector), and the real cost levers are quantization and hot/cold tiering, not vendor choice.

themes.theme: Collapse of the standalone vector-database category

insights.claim: The standalone vector database category has largely dissolved because approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search is now a native column/data type in general-purpose databases teams already run — Postgres, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, ClickHouse, MongoDB, and Redis — making the 'do I need a new database for this' question answer itself as 'no.'
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Bearish structural signal for pure-play standalone vector database vendors (Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate, Qdrant) as incumbent general-purpose databases have absorbed their core feature; competitive moat has shifted from 'having ANN at all' to operational/cost execution.
insights.quote: That moment has passed. Approximate nearest-neighbor search is now everywhere, and is more often than not a column type in the databases that teams already run
insights.locator: For a few years it looked like every AI stack

insights.claim: Pinecone launched its managed vector database service in 2021 and effectively named the category; Milvus, Weaviate, and Qdrant arrived around the same window, built on the premise that general-purpose databases lacked a good ANN index so semantic search needed a purpose-built home.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Establishes the founding thesis and timeline of the standalone vector-DB category that the article argues has since been undercut by incumbents.
insights.locator: The Category Collapsed Into The Engines You Already Run

insights.claim: Incumbent databases closed the ANN gap quickly and largely converged on the same algorithm: Elasticsearch shipped approximate k-NN over HNSW (building on Lucene's implementation); OpenSearch has had a k-NN plugin since its 1.0 release; pgvector added HNSW in version 0.5.0 (August 2023); MongoDB Atlas Vector Search reached general availability in December 2023; Redis exposed vector similarity in RediSearch 2.4 in 2022; and ClickHouse made HNSW vector similarity generally available in version 25.8 — with HNSW showing up everywhere because it delivers 95+ percent recall without a rebuild step.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Gives a precise timeline investors can use to date when each major database vendor became a credible vector-search competitor, useful for competitive-moat and market-share analysis of AI infrastructure incumbents vs. startups.
insights.locator: The incumbents closed that gap fast

insights.claim: The reason the standalone vector-DB category consolidated into general-purpose engines is not feature parity on paper but that production retrieval is rarely pure vector lookup: real systems combine lexical scoring, structured filters (tenant, language, ACL, freshness), and aggregations with dense retrieval and often rerank the merged set, all of which wants to live next to the vectors, and a separate vector database forces dual writes and a second consistency model to operate.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism behind vendor consolidation: operational complexity (dual writes, dual consistency) rather than raw recall performance is what killed the standalone category's differentiation, a durable structural reason unlikely to reverse.
insights.quote: A separate vector database forces dual writes, a second consistency model, and a second thing to page someone about at 3 AM.
insights.locator: The reason this consolidation stuck is not feature parity

themes.theme: Memory is the real cost driver

insights.claim: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is a graph index that must be traversed via pointer chasing, and that traversal is only fast when the graph and its vectors sit fully in RAM; once nodes spill to disk, latency becomes dominated by page faults rather than distance computation, so the dominant cost of vector search at scale is memory, which scales with vector count times dimensionality.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Core mental model for anyone budgeting vector-search infrastructure: cost is a memory-capacity problem, not a compute or vendor-licensing problem, so evaluate any vector product by its per-vector memory footprint math first.
insights.quote: the dominant cost of vector search at scale is memory, and memory scales with the product of vector count and dimensionality
insights.locator: What Actually Drives Cost: Memory Is The Whole Story

insights.claim: OpenSearch documents the per-vector memory footprint for an in-memory HNSW index as 1.1 × (4 × dimension + 8 × M) bytes per vector, where the 4×dimension term is the float32 vector itself, 8×M is the graph's per-node connection overhead, and the 1.1 factor is roughly 10 percent slack — meaning dimensionality, not document count alone, sets the required hardware tier.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: A concrete, reusable formula investors and engineers can apply directly to size and compare vector-search infrastructure costs across vendors, independent of marketing claims.
insights.locator: The per-vector memory footprint for an in-memory HNSW index is well defined

insights.claim: One million 1,536-dimension float32 vectors — the output size of OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large model — take about 6.1 GB before graph overhead; ten million of them need roughly 60 GB just for the vectors, all RAM-resident for predictable latency, turning a vector feature into a capacity-planning problem.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete, citable benchmark (60GB RAM per 10M embeddings at OpenAI's common embedding dimension) to sanity-check vector-search infrastructure spend or vendor pricing claims.

insights.claim: HNSW's graph structure compounds memory cost because it stores neighbor lists at every layer, so the index can run 2-5x the size of the raw vectors, whereas IVFFlat's flat per-cell storage stays near 1.1x — meaning the instinctive response to slow vector search (more shards, higher recall settings, bigger ef_search) often makes performance worse because each lever adds memory pressure, fan-out, or per-query CPU, and the slowest shard sets p99 latency at scale.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive operational warning: naive scaling responses to vector-search slowness (add shards, raise recall) typically backfire, which is a non-obvious risk for teams under latency SLA pressure making reactive infra decisions.

insights.claim: On standard ANN benchmarks, pushing HNSW recall from 95 percent to 100 percent can cost roughly 7x in throughput, meaning the last few points of recall are usually the most expensive part of the pipeline and rarely something users actually notice.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Quantifies a steep, non-linear recall/throughput tradeoff; teams should deliberately cap recall targets around 95 percent rather than chase perfection, since the marginal cost (7x throughput) vastly outweighs marginal user-perceived benefit.
insights.locator: The recall-versus-throughput curve is steep and non-linear

themes.theme: Quantization and tiering as the real cost levers

insights.claim: Quantization shrinks each vector's memory footprint by trading a controllable amount of precision for a large reduction in bytes, usually paired with a rescoring step that re-ranks top candidates using full-precision vectors held on cheaper storage; this is where real cost reduction happens, and it is mostly orthogonal to vendor choice.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Positions quantization strategy — not database vendor selection — as the primary lever engineering teams control for vector-search cost, reframing procurement priorities away from vendor lock-in debates.
insights.quote: This is where real cost reduction happens, and it is mostly orthogonal to vendor choice.
insights.locator: The Levers That Bend The Curve

insights.claim: Lucene's int8 scalar quantization cuts memory by about 75 percent while keeping raw vectors on disk for rescoring; binary quantization, which collapses each dimension to a single bit, reaches a 32x reduction and works well on high-dimensional embeddings with oversampling, with Qdrant reporting 0.98 recall@100 on 1536-dimension OpenAI embeddings using 4x oversampling; Elasticsearch's Better Binary Quantization took a 138-million-vector, 1024-dimension dataset from roughly 535 GB down to about 19 GB.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Gives specific, comparable compression benchmarks (75%, 32x, 535GB->19GB) that investors and engineers can use to evaluate vendor quantization claims against a known baseline.
insights.locator: The numbers behind these are concrete

insights.claim: Disk-based ANN keeps most of the index on SSD with only a compressed copy in memory: Microsoft's DiskANN can index a billion points on a single 64GB machine plus SSD at 95+ percent recall while serving thousands of queries per second, and Amazon's S3 Vectors targets up to 90 percent lower cost on large vector datasets by trading latency for price.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Identifies billion-scale, cost-optimized vector search as now achievable on commodity single-machine hardware plus object storage — a meaningful cost deflation datapoint for large-scale AI retrieval infrastructure spend.
insights.locator: The other lever is admitting that not all vectors deserve RAM

insights.claim: The latency trade from moving vectors off RAM is real and measurable: OpenSearch's disk-based mode showed p90 latency of 96 milliseconds versus 24 milliseconds for the in-memory path; that gap is invisible for agentic retrieval inside a multi-second reasoning loop but disqualifying for interactive autocomplete, so the design move at billion-scale is tiering — hot vectors in RAM-backed HNSW, cold vectors quantized on disk or object storage — while AWS S3 Vectors and Turbopuffer aim to offer both large scale and low cost at decent performance simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete decision framework (96ms vs 24ms p90) for matching vector-search architecture to use case latency tolerance — agentic/batch workloads can go cold-tier for major cost savings, interactive UX cannot.
insights.locator: The trade is real and measurable

insights.claim: Because engines have converged on the same HNSW algorithm and the same compression toolkit, the self-managed versus managed decision is no longer about capability — both can do HNSW, quantize, and tier — but about who owns three things: the memory-sizing math, the rescoring and latency cliff, and the routing between hot and cold tiers.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Reframes vector-database vendor evaluation around operational ownership rather than feature checklists, which is the more durable and decision-useful axis for buyers.
insights.locator: Where The Self-Managed Versus Managed Line Really Falls

insights.claim: Managed vector-search services earn their margin by absorbing the provisioning problem: they size RAM, isolate vector traffic onto dedicated nodes so it doesn't contend with operational queries (MongoDB shipped dedicated Search Nodes alongside its Vector Search GA for this reason), and hide the cold-tier fetch behind a single API, in exchange for giving up some tuning knobs and paying a margin.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Explains the concrete value proposition (dedicated node isolation, hidden cold-tier complexity) that justifies managed vector-search service margins.
insights.locator: Managed services earn their keep by absorbing the provisioning problem

insights.claim: The decision between managed and self-managed vector search reduces to two questions: does the vector data already live in an operational store the team runs (so adding a column avoids a whole second system), and what is the latency SLO against the cost ceiling — teams with a strict sub-20 millisecond interactive budget and a small ops crew are usually better served by a managed hot tier, while teams already running Postgres or OpenSearch at scale with headcount to own capacity planning will get more out of self-managing quantization and tiering directly.
insights.speaker: Itamar Syn-Hershko
insights.so_what: Actionable buy-vs-build heuristic for any team architecting AI retrieval infrastructure: use existing operational-store presence and a sub-20ms latency threshold as the deciding variables, not vendor marketing.
insights.quote: Pick the engine for the workload, not the other way around.
insights.locator: The decision driver is rarely the technology
